summary: Specifies updated procedures for handling Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) traffic in Ethernet VPNs, including selective multicast and segmentation of provider tunnels. It updates RFC 7432.

plainLanguage.summary: Some messages have to reach many receivers at once. This document updates how Ethernet VPNs carry that traffic, and how a long provider tunnel can be split into shorter segments.

questions: what is an s-pmsi a-d route
subtitle: Fills the gaps in how Ethernet VPNs deliver broadcast and multicast traffic, with selective and segmented tunnels.

tldr.problem: RFC 7432 defines how Ethernet VPNs handle Broadcast, Unknown Unicast and Multicast traffic, but leaves gaps around selective tunnels and tunnel segmentation across ASes and regions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9572 reuses the VPLS and MVPN procedures with EVPN-specific differences, and adds three EVPN route types: Per-Region I-PMSI A-D (9), S-PMSI A-D (10) and Leaf A-D (11).
tldr.outcome: EVPN operators can send multicast only to interested PEs and can split provider tunnels at AS or region borders. The document updates RFC 7432.

today: RFC 9572 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024 that updates RFC 7432. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Adds to EVPN
sections.content:
RFC 7117 specifies procedures for multicast in the Virtual Private LAN Service, using both inclusive tunnels and selective tunnels with or without inter-AS segmentation, similar to the Multicast VPN procedures of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514. RFC 7524 specifies inter-area tunnel segmentation procedures for both VPLS multicast and MVPNs.

RFC 7432 specifies BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN procedures, including those handling Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast traffic. It refers to RFC 7117 for details but leaves a few feature gaps related to selective tunnels and tunnel segmentation. This document fills those gaps by covering the use of selective and segmented tunnels in EVPNs. In the same way that RFC 7432 refers to RFC 7117 for details, this document only specifies differences from the relevant procedures, rather than repeating their text, and those differences are applicable to EVPNs only.

MVPN, VPLS and EVPN technologies all need to discover other Provider Edges in the same VPN and announce the inclusive tunnels. MVPN introduced the Inclusive P-Multicast Service Interface concept and uses I-PMSI Auto-Discovery routes for that purpose. EVPN uses Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag A-D routes, while VPLS adds a PMSI Tunnel Attribute to an existing VPLS A-D route. For selective tunnels all three use the same term, Selective PMSI A-D routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The base EVPN specification borrowed its multicast procedures from an older service and left some gaps. This document closes them, by listing what is different when the same procedures are used in EVPN.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The document assumes the reader is familiar with MVPN, VPLS multicast and EVPN, but it restates the terms it needs.

A PMSI is a conceptual interface for a PE to send customer multicast traffic to all or some PEs in the same VPN. An I-PMSI is an inclusive PMSI, which enables traffic to be sent to all PEs in the same VPN. An S-PMSI is a selective PMSI, which enables traffic to be sent to some of the PEs in the same VPN. An I/S-PMSI A-D route is the auto-discovery route used to announce the tunnels that instantiate an I-PMSI or an S-PMSI.

An IMET A-D route is the EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag A-D route, the EVPN equivalent of the MVPN intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route. An SMET A-D route is the Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag A-D route of RFC 9251, the EVPN equivalent of an MVPN Leaf A-D route, but unsolicited and untargeted. A Leaf A-D route exists for explicit leaf-tracking purposes: it is triggered by an I/S-PMSI A-D route, is targeted at the advertiser of that route, and embeds the entire NLRI of the triggering route.

The PMSI Tunnel Attribute is an optional transitive BGP attribute that may be attached to PMSI and Leaf A-D routes to give information about a PMSI tunnel. The document also uses the usual terms for autonomous systems, internal and external BGP, and Route Targets, which control route importation and propagation.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of route carry the multicast information: one that says where to send everything, one that says where to send a particular flow, and one that says which devices actually want it.

sections.title: Tunnel Segmentation
sections.content:
Provider tunnels for MVPN, EVPN and VPLS BUM traffic can be segmented for technical or administrative reasons. The MVPN and VPLS documents cover inter-AS segmentation, and RFC 7524 covers inter-area segmentation. With tunnel segmentation, different segments of an end-to-end tunnel may have different encapsulation overheads, but the largest overhead of a tunnel caused by an encapsulation method on a particular segment is no different from the case of a non-segmented tunnel with that method.

Segmentation may be required or desired for several reasons. A service may span multiple providers, and the end-to-end provider tunnels have to be segmented at and stitched by the border routers, because different providers may use different tunnel technologies, and even with the same technology it may be impractical to set up tunnels across provider boundaries. The same applies between the autonomous systems or areas of a single provider, where a backbone area may use one tunnel technology while other areas use another.

Segmentation can also be used to divide an autonomous system or area into smaller regions, so that control plane state and forwarding plane state are limited to those of individual regions. Instead of replicating to 100 PEs in the entire AS, a PE only needs to replicate to local PEs and border routers, which then replicate onward. This reduces the forwarding plane burden and also reduces the leaf-tracking burden in the control plane.

Smaller regions also help tunnel aggregation, because it becomes easier to find congruence among the segments of different constituent tunnels, so fewer leaves of the base tunnel have to discard traffic. And smaller regions give smaller Bit Index Explicit Replication subdomains, so smaller BitStrings can be used without sending multiple copies of the same packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting a long tunnel into pieces at borders lets each piece use whatever technology that part of the network prefers, and keeps the amount of state each device holds smaller.

sections.title: Three New EVPN Route Types
sections.content:
The EVPN NLRI format has a route type field of one octet, a length field of one octet, and a variable route-type-specific part. Eight route types had been defined in RFC 7432, RFC 9136 and RFC 9251: Ethernet Auto-discovery, MAC/IP Advertisement, Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag, Ethernet Segment, IP Prefix, Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag Route, Multicast Membership Report Synch Route, and Multicast Leave Synch Route.

This document defines three more. Route type 9 is the Per-Region I-PMSI A-D route, whose route-type-specific part holds a Route Distinguisher of 8 octets, an Ethernet Tag ID of 4 octets and a Region ID of 8 octets. The Region ID identifies the region and is encoded in the same way as an extended community. Route type 10 is the S-PMSI A-D route, which adds an Ethernet Tag ID and an Originator's Addr Length field to the S-PMSI A-D route of RFC 7117, with the granularity level per Ethernet Tag. Route type 11 is the Leaf A-D route, whose route-type-specific part holds the route key, the NLRI of the route for which the Leaf A-D route was generated, followed by the Originator's Addr Length and the Originator's Addr.

A Leaf A-D route is originated in response to a PMSI route, which could be an IMET A-D route, a per-region I-PMSI A-D route, an S-PMSI A-D route, or another route type defined in the future. The route-type-specific part of the type 9 and type 10 routes starts with a Type 1 Route Distinguisher whose Administrator sub-field MUST match that of the RD in all current EVPN routes that are not Leaf A-D routes, that is, the non-Leaf A-D routes from the same advertising router for a given EVPN instance.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new kinds of route are added, one for each job: announcing a region's tunnels, announcing a selective tunnel for a particular flow, and reporting back which devices want that flow.

sections.title: Selective Multicast
sections.content:
RFC 9251 specifies procedures for EVPN selective forwarding of IP multicast traffic using SMET routes. It assumes that selective forwarding is always used with ingress replication for all flows. A Network Virtualization Edge proxies the IGMP and MLD state that it learns on its attachment circuits into SMET routes advertised to other NVEs, and a receiving NVE converts the SMET routes back into IGMP and MLD messages and sends them out of its attachment circuits.

With those procedures, selective forwarding is done for all flows and the SMET routes are advertised for all flows. An operator may not want to track all those source and group states on the NVEs, since the multicast traffic pattern allows inclusive forwarding for most flows while selective forwarding is needed only for a few high-rate flows. For that reason, or for tunnel types other than ingress replication or BIER, the S-PMSI and Leaf A-D procedures defined for selective multicast for VPLS in RFC 7117 are used. In short, a source NVE advertises S-PMSI A-D routes to announce the tunnels used for certain flows, and receiving NVEs either join the announced tunnel or respond with Leaf A-D routes if the L flag is set in the S-PMSI A-D route's PMSI Tunnel Attribute, so that the source NVE can include them as tunnel leaves.

An optimization may be applied. Even if a source NVE sets the L flag to request Leaf A-D routes, an egress NVE MAY omit the Leaf A-D route if it has already advertised a corresponding SMET route, and the source NVE MUST use that in its place. The optional optimizations specified for MVPNs in RFC 8534 are also applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: Most multicast traffic can go to everyone. For the few flows that are expensive, the sender can ask who actually wants them and build a tunnel only to those who answered.

sections.title: Inter-AS Segmentation
sections.content:
The inter-AS procedures of RFC 7117 differ from the EVPN ones. In VPLS, if several border routers in an AS receive the same inter-AS A-D route, the best route procedures ensure that only one of them propagates the route in internal BGP, and that one becomes the root of the intra-AS segment. For EVPNs a different approach is used: each border router re-advertises its received inter-AS A-D route to its internal BGP peers and becomes the root of an intra-AS segment of the inter-AS tree, and the segments rooted at different border routers are disjoint from each other.

The PMSI Tunnel Attribute MUST specify the tunnel for the segment. If, and only if, the border router needs to know the leaves of the tree in order to establish the tunnel, it MUST set the L flag to 1 in the attribute to trigger Leaf A-D routes from egress PEs and downstream border routers, and it MUST be configured with an import Route Target, which controls acceptance of Leaf A-D routes by the border router.

If a received inter-AS A-D route has the L flag set, a receiving PE MUST originate a corresponding Leaf A-D route. A receiving border router MUST originate one if and only if it received and imported one or more corresponding Leaf A-D routes from its downstream peers, or if it has non-null downstream forwarding state for the tunnel that instantiates its downstream intra-AS segment.

An ingress PE does not set the L flag in its IMET A-D route's attribute, even with ingress replication tunnels, because it does not rely on Leaf A-D routes to discover leaves in its AS. With segmentation, an ingress PE MUST determine the leaves in its AS from the BGP next hops in all its received IMET A-D routes. PEs within the same AS all have different next hops and are all considered leaves, and PEs from other autonomous systems have the next hop set to the address of a border router in the local AS, so only those border routers are considered as leaves, acting as proxies for the PEs in other autonomous systems.
sections.plainLanguage: When a tunnel crosses an autonomous system boundary, the border routers on each side keep their own segment of it. Each side works out its own downstream devices from the next hops in the routes it received.

sections.title: Inter-Region Segmentation
sections.content:
RFC 7524 addresses inter-area segmentation and does not explicitly cover EVPNs. However, if 'area' is replaced by 'region' and 'ABR' by 'RBR', a Regional Border Router, everything still works and can be applied to EVPNs as well. A region can be a sub-area, or it can be an entire autonomous system including its external links. Instead of being defined automatically from IGP areas, a region is defined as a BGP peer group.

Because every I-PMSI route from each PE is propagated throughout all the autonomous systems or regions, and may also trigger corresponding Leaf A-D routes, this can result in too many routes and tunnels. The I-PMSI routes from all PEs in an autonomous system or region can be aggregated into a single I-PMSI route originated from the RBRs, and traffic from all those individual I-PMSI tunnels is switched into the single I-PMSI tunnel. The per-PE I-PMSI routes are not propagated to other regions. If multiple RBRs are connected to a region, each advertises such a route with the same Region ID and Ethernet Tag ID.

Unlike MVPNs, EVPNs do not aggregate S-PMSI routes, because the number of PEs that advertise S-PMSI routes for the same source and group pair is small.

The Region ID is encoded like an extended community. It can encode an autonomous system number, using a Transitive Two-Octet or Four-Octet AS-specific extended community of sub-type 0x09 with the Global Administrator set to the AS number and the Local Administrator set to 0, or an area ID, using a Transitive IPv4-Address-specific extended community with the Global Administrator set to the area ID and the Local Administrator set to 0.

For EVPNs it is perfectly fine to change the next hop when an RBR re-advertises the routes, instead of relying on the Segmented Next-Hop Extended Community that RFC 7524 requires. This document therefore specifies that RBRs change the BGP next hop and do not use the S-NH-EC, so that neither ingress nor egress PEs need to understand it, and the same procedure based on BGP next hops is used for both inter-AS and inter-region segmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of splitting the network at area borders, the split can be at any border, including the edge of a whole autonomous system. Each region then announces one tunnel for all its devices, rather than one per device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures for selective forwarding via S-PMSI and Leaf A-D routes are based on the same procedures as those used for MVPNs and VPLS multicast, and the procedures for tunnel segmentation are based on similar procedures used for MVPN inter-AS and inter-area tunnel segmentation and for VPLS multicast inter-AS tunnel segmentation. When applied to EVPNs, they do not introduce new security concerns beyond those already discussed in RFC 6513, RFC 6514, RFC 7117 and RFC 7524, and they do not introduce new security concerns compared to RFC 7432.

One point from the multihoming section is worth repeating here. To support multihoming with segmentation, Ethernet Segment Identifier labels SHOULD be allocated from a Domain-wide Common Block for all tunnel types, including ingress replication tunnels. Peers then know that the ESI labels come from that block, and the existing multihoming procedures work as they are, whether a multihomed Ethernet segment spans segmentation regions or not.
sections.plainLanguage: The procedures are borrowed from older services, so they bring the same security considerations with them and add none of their own.

items.title: I-PMSI
items.text: Inclusive PMSI. Enables traffic to be sent to all PEs in the same VPN.

items.title: S-PMSI
items.text: Selective PMSI. Enables traffic to be sent to some of the PEs in the same VPN.

items.title: IMET A-D route
items.text: The EVPN route that announces the tunnels carrying traffic to every PE.

items.title: SMET A-D route
items.text: The EVPN route that announces selective forwarding for IP multicast.

items.title: Leaf A-D route
items.text: Sent back to the advertiser of a PMSI route to say that this PE wants to receive that traffic.

viz.caption: WHY A TUNNEL IS SPLIT INTO SEGMENTS (RFC 9572, SECTION 2.1)

items.title: Different tunnel technologies
items.text: Each provider may use a different one, and it may be impractical to set tunnels up across provider boundaries.

items.title: Less state to hold
items.text: Control plane and forwarding state are limited to the size of a region rather than the whole AS.

items.title: Less replication
items.text: A PE replicates to local PEs and border routers, which then replicate onward.

items.title: Better aggregation
items.text: Smaller regions make it easier to match tunnel segments, so less traffic is discarded.

items.title: Smaller BIER subdomains
items.text: Smaller BitStrings mean a packet need not be sent several times.
